sections.title: Noticing the world
sections.description: Can you tell living things from things that are not alive, and use your senses to notice the world?

sections.title: Materials around me
sections.description: Do you know what everyday things are made of, and how they feel when you touch them?

sections.title: Asking questions
sections.description: Can you look closely and try things out to find answers, just like a scientist?

questions.question: Which of these is a living thing?
questions.options: a spoon | a rock | a chair | a cat
questions.explanation: A cat is alive — it eats, moves and grows. A rock, a chair and a spoon do not eat or grow, so they are not living.

questions.question: A little plant is living. What does a living plant do that a toy plant never does?
questions.options: it needs batteries | it stays the same forever | it grows | it is made in a shop
questions.explanation: Living things grow. A real plant gets bigger and makes new leaves, but a toy plant stays the same forever.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT living?
questions.options: a bird | a tree | a fish | a teddy bear
questions.explanation: A teddy bear cannot eat, grow or move by itself, so it is not living. Birds, fish and trees are all alive.

questions.question: Which part of your body do you use to see a rainbow?
questions.options: your ears | your nose | your eyes | your feet
questions.explanation: We see with our eyes. Your ears hear, your nose smells, and your feet help you walk and run.

questions.question: You hear a bird singing in a tree. Which part of your body are you using?
questions.options: your hands | your ears | your tongue | your eyes
questions.explanation: We hear sounds with our ears. The bird's song travels through the air right into them!

questions.question: A window lets you see right through it. Which material is a window made of?
questions.explanation: Windows are made of glass because we can see through it. Wood, wool and stone are not see-through.

questions.question: Which of these feels soft when you touch it?
questions.options: a glass cup | a stone | a metal spoon | a wool jumper
questions.explanation: Wool is soft and squashy — that is why jumpers keep us cosy. Stone, metal and glass all feel hard.

questions.question: A carpenter cuts a tree to make a chair. Which material is the chair made of?
questions.explanation: Trees give us wood, and wood is strong enough to make chairs, tables and doors.

questions.question: You dip your hand in a puddle of water. Which word tells how the water feels?
questions.explanation: Water feels wet! Hard is how a stone feels, furry is like a cat, and crunchy is how a biscuit sounds.

questions.question: Sara wants to know which of two cups holds more water. What should she do?
questions.options: close her eyes | pour water into both cups and look carefully | ask the cat | just guess
questions.correctAnswer: pour water into both cups and look carefully
questions.explanation: Scientists try things out and look carefully. Pouring water into both cups shows Sara the answer for real.

questions.question: Omar wonders if a seed will grow into a plant. What is the best way to find out?
questions.options: hide the seed in a drawer | plant it, water it and watch what happens | throw the seed away | eat the seed
questions.correctAnswer: plant it, water it and watch what happens
questions.explanation: To find out, Omar can try it and watch! Planting and watering the seed lets him see with his own eyes if it grows.

questions.question: Amina looks very closely at a ladybird and counts its spots. What is Amina doing?
questions.options: singing a song | observing like a scientist | cooking dinner | sleeping
questions.explanation: Looking closely and counting is called observing — it is one of the most important things a scientist does.
